Prevention models and frameworks

What Works

Youth homelessness prevention does not depend on one program, one policy, or one sector. The strongest approaches combine early identification, relational support, school-community coordination, family and natural supports, housing stability, and policy alignment.

Use the filters to compare prevention approaches and open each model page for source-linked context.
Informational note

This page is informational and educational only. Please review the linked sources and confirm decisions with qualified professionals, local services, and appropriate organizations.

School-community early intervention

The Community of Schools and Services (COSS) Model

A school-linked, place-based early intervention model that integrates risk identification, referral pathways, family-centered support, community coordination, and outcomes monitoring.

Open model page

Early intervention and relational support

Reconnect / Youth Reconnect

Reconnect focuses on young people who are at risk of, or in early stages of, homelessness by supporting reconnection to family, school, community, and natural supports.

Open model page

Systematic school-based risk identification

The Upstream Project

Tools such as Upstream are designed to help schools identify hidden homelessness and early risk more systematically, rather than relying only on visible crisis or informal concern.

Open model page

Relational prevention

Family and Natural Supports

Family and Natural Supports approaches strengthen safe relationships with family, chosen family, kin, mentors, and trusted adults.

Open model page

Housing stabilization and recurrence prevention

Housing First for Youth (HF4Y)

HF4Y is a youth-focused housing and support model that helps young people exit homelessness and transition toward adulthood.

Open model page

Education rights and school stability

McKinney-Vento Act in the United States

McKinney-Vento shows how education systems can carry explicit responsibilities for students experiencing homelessness.

Open model page

Youth protection and policy pathway

Washington’s Senate Bill 6560 and Youth Homelessness Prevention

Washington’s Senate Bill 6560 shows how prevention can become state legislation by creating clearer public-system responsibility before harm deepens.

Open model page

Rights-based policy responsibility

Duty to Assist: A Human Rights Approach to Youth Homelessness

Duty to Assist is a rights-based prevention approach that would require public authorities to make reasonable efforts to help young people avoid homelessness or stabilize housing before crisis deepens.

Open model page

Basic needs and school belonging

Breakfast Programs and School Food Security

Food programs can reduce immediate barriers to learning and reveal broader material hardship that may require school-community support.

Open model page

Teacher education and institutional recognition

Critical Pedagogy and Culturally Responsive Practice

Critical pedagogy helps educators examine power, poverty, exclusion, voice, and lived experience in how schools interpret student struggle.
